title: Car Trouble on Mombasa Road
culturalNote: Breaking down is a shared Kenyan experience — strangers stop, someone knows a mechanic (fundi), and a tow truck appears faster than you'd expect. Kenyans treat gari (car) as n/n: "gari yangu imeharibika" (my car has broken down), where Sanifu says "gari langu limeharibika". The subjunctive shows up whenever you ask, suggest or arrange: "nimpigie fundi?" (shall I call a mechanic?), "tungoje hapa" (let's wait here).
startingPoint: Your car stalls on the shoulder of Mombasa Road. A passing motorist, Mwangi, pulls over.

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.english: Sorry, boss! Has your car broken down?

words.gloss: boss — friendly, informal way to address a man (driver, guard, waiter) — m/wa noun (people & animals)
"has broken down" — i- (it, n/n) + -me- + -haribika. Kenyan agreement for gari.

turns.speaker: Wewe
turns.swahili: Ndiyo. Ilikuwa inaenda vizuri, halafu ghafla ikazima.
turns.english: Yes. It was going fine, then suddenly it stalled.

words.gloss: "It was" — i- (subject: it (n/n)) + li- (past) + -wa (be). From kuwa.
"It is going" — i- (subject: it (n/n)) + na- (present) + -enda (go). From kuenda.

options.swahili: Ndiyo. Ilikuwa inaenda vizuri, halafu ghafla ikazima.
Ndiyo. Itakuwa inaenda vizuri, halafu ghafla ikazima.
Hapana. Ilikuwa inaenda vizuri, halafu ghafla ikazima.

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.swahili: Ebu nione. Hmm, sijui shida ni nini. Nimpigie fundi wangu?
turns.english: Let me see. Hmm, I don't know what the problem is. Shall I call my mechanic?

words.gloss: come on / let's — softens a request
"Let me see / should I see?" — ni- (subject: I) + -one (see, subjunctive -e). From kuona.
"I don't know" — si- (negative subject: not I) + -jui (know, negative ends in -i). From kujua.
problem / trouble — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
"my" — m/wa agreement (for people: mtoto wangu, watoto wangu).

conjugation.tense: my · your · his/her · our · your (pl.) · their

turns.speaker: Wewe
turns.swahili: Ndiyo, tafadhali. Mpigie! Sijui fundi yeyote hapa.
turns.english: Yes, please. Call him! I don't know any mechanic here.

words.gloss: "Call him/her!" — m- (object: him/her) + -pigie (call, subjunctive -e: polite command). From kupigia. Extension: prepositional (-ia/-ea: "for / to / at").
"I don't know" — si- (negative subject: not I) + -jui (know, negative ends in -i). From kujua.

options.swahili: Ndiyo, tafadhali. Mpigie! Sijui fundi yeyote hapa.
Ndiyo, tafadhali. Nipigie! Sijui fundi yeyote hapa.
Ndiyo, tafadhali. Mpigie! Najua fundi yeyote hapa.

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.swahili: Sawa. Amesema atakuja baada ya dakika thelathini.
turns.english: Okay. He says he'll come in thirty minutes.

words.gloss: "He/she has said" — a- (subject: he/she) + me- (perfect (done / now-state)) + -sema (say). From kusema.
"He/she will come" — a- (subject: he/she) + ta- (future) + -ja (come). From kuja.
minute — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
30 (n/n form — used for counting, money, things)

turns.speaker: Wewe
turns.swahili: Thelathini? Tusubiri hapa, au twende kwenye kivuli?
turns.english: Thirty? Should we wait here, or go into the shade?

words.gloss: 30 (n/n form — used for counting, money, things)
"Let's go" — tw- (subject: we) + -ende (go, subjunctive -e). From kuenda.
"at / on / in / to" — the all-purpose place word (kwenye meza = on the table).

options.swahili: Thelathini? Tusubiri hapa, au twende kwenye kivuli?
Thelathini? Tunasubiri hapa, au twende kwenye kivuli?
Thelathini? Tusubiri hapa, au tuende kwenye maji?

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.swahili: Twende kwenye kivuli. Jua ni kali.
turns.english: Let's go into the shade. The sun is strong.

words.gloss: "Let's go" — tw- (subject: we) + -ende (go, subjunctive -e). From kuenda.
"at / on / in / to" — the all-purpose place word (kwenye meza = on the table).
sun — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
"fierce / sharp / strict / spicy" — n/n agreement (things; Kenyans use it for most non-people nouns).

turns.speaker: Wewe
turns.swahili: Na kama fundi hawezi kuitengeneza hapa?
turns.english: And if the mechanic can't fix it here?

words.gloss: "He/she cannot" — ha- (negative subject: not he/she) + -wezi (can, negative ends in -i). From kuweza.
"To fix it" — ku- (infinitive "to") + i- (object: it) + -tengeneza (fix). From kutengeneza.

options.swahili: Na kama fundi hawezi kuitengeneza hapa?
Na kama fundi anaweza kuitengeneza hapa?
Na kama fundi hawezi kunitengeneza hapa?

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.swahili: Basi inabidi tumwambie aivute mpaka gereji yake.
turns.english: Then we'll have to tell him to tow it to his garage.

words.gloss: so / well then / okay, that's it
"It is necessary" — i- (subject: it (n/n)) + na- (present) + -bidi (be necessary). From kubidi.
"Let's tell him/her" — tu- (subject: we) + mw- (object: him/her) + -ambie (tell, subjunctive -e). From kuambia.
border / boundary (also: until) (plural mipaka) — Kenyans give it n/n agreement
words.sanifu: Sanifu: m/mi class — mpaka wa shamba

words.gloss: "his/her" — n/n singular agreement (nyumba yake). In Kenyan speech also used for family words and most things (jina yake, gari yake).

conjugation.tense: my · your · his/her · our · your (pl.) · their

turns.speaker: Wewe
turns.swahili: Sawa. Naomba umwambie anipigie simu akifika.
turns.english: Okay. Please tell him to call me when he arrives.

words.gloss: "I ask for" — na- (short for nina-: I + present) + -omba (ask for). From kuomba.
"(please) tell him/her" — u- (subject: you) + mw- (object: him/her) + -ambie (tell, subjunctive -e). From kuambia.
"He/she should call me" — a- (subject: he/she) + ni- (object: me) + -pigie (call, subjunctive -e). From kupigia. Extension: prepositional (-ia/-ea: "for / to / at").
phone / call — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
"If/when he/she arrives" — a- (subject: he/she) + ki- (if / when · or "-ing" after kuwa) + -fika (arrive). From kufika. After a past kuwa (nilikuwa …) the -ki- form means "…-ing".

options.swahili: Sawa. Naomba umwambie anipigie simu akifika.
Sawa. Naomba uniambie anipigie simu akifika.
Sawa. Naomba umwambie nimpigie simu akifika.

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.swahili: Hakuna shida. Usijali, Nairobi ni hivi tu.
turns.english: No problem. Don't worry, that's just Nairobi.

turns.speaker: Wewe
turns.swahili: Ninakushukuru sana kwa kunisaidia. Nikulipe kitu?
turns.english: I'm very grateful to you for helping me. Shall I give you something?

words.gloss: "Let me pay you / should I pay you?" — ni- (subject: I) + ku- (object: you) + -lipe (pay, subjunctive -e). From kulipa.
thing (plural vitu) — Kenyans give it n/n agreement
words.sanifu: Sanifu: ki/vi class — kitu changu, vitu vyangu

options.swahili: Ninakushukuru sana kwa kunisaidia. Nikulipe kitu?
Ninakushukuru sana kwa kunisaidia. Unilipe kitu?
Unanishukuru sana kwa kunisaidia. Nikulipe kitu?

turns.speaker: Mwangi
turns.swahili: Hapana, usinilipe! Leo ni wewe, kesho ni mimi.
turns.english: No, don't pay me! Today it's you, tomorrow it's me.

words.gloss: today — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
tomorrow — n/n noun (same word for one & many)

vocabulary.exampleContext: The most useful subjunctive in Kenya

vocabulary.swahili: Leo ni wewe, kesho ni mimi

practice.explanation: Kenyans treat gari as n/n (i-). Sanifu: gari lako limeharibika.
Nipigie = "Call me!" — ni- (object: me) + -pigie (call, subjunctive -e: polite command). From kupigia. Extension: prepositional (-ia/-ea: "for / to / at").
subiri doesn't end in -a, so its subjunctive looks the same: tusubiri.
Twende = "Let's go" — tw- (subject: we) + -ende (go, subjunctive -e). From kuenda.
Atakuja = "He/she will come" — a- (subject: he/she) + ta- (future) + -ja (come). From kuja.
ha- (not he) + -wez- + -i. Kuitengeneza = to fix it (-i- = it).
Second verb in subjunctive: a- + -ni- + -pigi- + -e = (that) he call me.

options.feedback: nimwambie = Let me tell him/her / should I tell him/her?
Nimlipe = Let me pay him/her / should I pay him/her?

practice.explanation: Nikulipe = "Let me pay you / should I pay you?" — ni- (subject: I) + ku- (object: you) + -lipe (pay, subjunctive -e). From kulipa.

practice.english: Today it's you, tomorrow it's me.
practice.explanation: A Kenyan way of saying "we all need help sometimes".
